title: I am the resurrection (John 11:17–27)
hook: grieving Martha makes a great confession of faith
tomorrow: The house filled with the odor

segments.voice: Yesterday, kalos, the good shepherd who calls his own by name. Your line was he knows my name. Whose name did you say on purpose? Day five hundred thirteen.

At hospital bedsides and after funerals, one sentence keeps coming back. If only. If only the ambulance had come sooner. If only I'd called. If only you'd been here. It isn't really a question, and it isn't quite blame. It's love with nowhere to go. In Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, a man named Lazarus has died, and his sister Martha hears that Jesus is finally on the road. She doesn't wait at the house. She goes out to meet him, and the first thing she says is that sentence.
screen: `IF ONLY.` → `LAZARUS IS DEAD.` → `MARTHA GOES OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: John says Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days. Friends have come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters. Mary stays sitting in the house. Martha gets up and goes. And she says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Then, in the same breath, she adds that even now she knows God will give him whatever he asks. Grief and trust, side by side, in one speech. Jesus tells her, your brother will rise again. She answers like a believer of her time: I know he will rise again at the resurrection on the last day. True, but far off. And then Jesus pulls the far-off thing into the present tense: "I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me, although he be dead, shall live." Not, I will bring the resurrection someday. I am it, standing here. He asks her straight out: believest thou this? And Martha, still grieving, answers with a full confession of faith. She says, yea, Lord, I have believed that thou art Christ the Son of the living God. Some readers set it beside Peter's confession in Matthew, which uses the same titles. Here it comes from a grieving woman on the road outside her village. Martha has a reputation, from Luke, as the busy sister who asked Jesus to send Mary to help her serve. John shows her another way: the one who walks out to meet him and says who he is. The Church offers these words among the readings for funeral Masses, and now keeps one memorial for Martha, Mary and Lazarus together.
screen: `FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB.` · `IF THOU HADST BEEN HERE.` · `NOT SOMEDAY: I AM.` · `MARTHA'S CONFESSION.` · then, large: `I AM THE RESURRECTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring to mind someone who has died. A grandparent, a friend, someone you hardly knew but think about. See their face, or their handwriting, or the chair they sat in. Let yourself feel the if only, if there is one. You don't have to fix it. Then, if you pray, you can say Martha's words for them, or Jesus's: I am the resurrection and the life. If you don't pray, simply hold their name and let it rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Anastasis. The Greek word for resurrection, literally a standing up again: what Jesus told Martha he was, standing right in front of her. Today's word.
Your line: love with nowhere to go. Today, if you pass a cemetery, a memorial or an old photo, pause for one breath and remember a name. Day five hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: John 11 is among the Gospel readings the Church provides for funeral Masses, and Catholics pray for their dead by name, especially in November and on the anniversary of a death.

myth: Martha only appears in the Gospels as the busy one in the kitchen
in John 11 she says: thou art Christ the Son of the living God.
Martha already believed in a resurrection on the last day
she says so; Jesus answers, I am the resurrection.
Martha's first words to Jesus mix grief and trust
if thou hadst been here, then: even now God will give thee what thou ask.

fork.setup: you're Martha. your brother has been dead four days, and Jesus has finally arrived. what do you do?
options: stay in the house with the mourners.
go out to meet him on the road.
send word that it's too late.
fork.reveal: Martha goes out to meet him while Mary stays in the house. on that road she says, thou art Christ the Son of the living God.

original.note: Greek: the resurrection, literally a standing up again (John 11:25).

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise about life after death, someday.
what it means: Jesus moves the resurrection from a far-off day into his own person, present tense: I am.
what a scholar hears: anastasis means a standing up again; Martha's confession in John 11:27 echoes the titles Peter uses in Matthew 16:16.

notes: Martha's confession (11:27) is given in paraphrase close to the Douay wording, without quotation marks.
